questions.explanation:
Why This Is Asked
- Tests practical CKAD skills: PVC-based file intake, in-cluster validation, batch processing, and external posting. Includes init tooling, secret handling, TLS rotation, and network policies.

Key Concepts
- PVC-based file discovery in a Deployment
- InitContainer for tooling installation
- kubectl dry-run validation and yamllint
- Batch processing controlled by a ConfigMap value
- Secrets for API credentials and TLS sidecar rotation
- NetworkPolicy scoping to internal endpoints
- Rollback and observability strategies

Code Example
```yaml
# Minimal skeleton for the auditor Deployment
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: auditor
  namespace: audit
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: auditor
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: auditor
    spec:
      volumes:
        - name: audits
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: audits-pvc
        - name: config
          configMap:
            name: audit-config
      initContainers:
        - name: prep-tools
          image: alpine:3.18
          command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache kubectl yamllint curl; sleep 0"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: audits
              mountPath: /audits
      containers:
        - name: auditor
          image: registry.example/auditor:latest
          volumeMounts:
            - name: audits
              mountPath: /audits
            - name: config
              mountPath: /etc/audit
          env:
            - name: AUDIT_ENDPOINT
              value: "http://audit-portal:8080/api/v1/audit"
          readinessProbe: {"tcpSocket": {"port": 8080}, "initialDelaySeconds": 15, "periodSeconds": 10}
          livenessProbe: {"tcpSocket": {"port": 8080}, "initialDelaySeconds": 30, "periodSeconds": 20}
      tolerations: []
```

Follow-up Questions
- How would you test under load and simulate a rollback?
- What metrics and logs would you collect to verify correctness?

## Why This Is Asked
CKAD fundamentals: volumes, InitContainers, ConfigMaps, Secrets, sidecars, network policies, and health checks in a per-namespace scope.

## Key Concepts
- Tail logs from a PVC-mounted path and write sanitized output back to the same volume
- Use a ConfigMap for PII redaction patterns
- Secure API credentials via a Secret and post summaries to an internal endpoint
- InitContainer installs tooling; sidecar rotates TLS certs
- NetworkPolicy confines egress to the internal log portal; readiness and liveness probes validate health

## Code Example
```yaml
# Minimal skeleton for the Deployment
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: log-redact
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: log-redact
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: log-redact
    spec:
      initContainers:
        - name: install-tools
          image: alpine:3.18
          command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache sed ripgrep"]
      containers:
        - name: redactor
          image: your-registry/log-redact:latest
          volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
            - name: patterns
              mountPath: /patterns
          env:
            - name: POST_URL
              value: "http://logportal:8080/api/v1/sanitize"
      volumes:
        - name: logs
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: logs-pvc
        - name: patterns
          configMap:
            name: redaction-config
```

Why This Is Asked
- Tests ability to wire ConfigMaps and Secrets across a namespace, plus InitContainer usage and lifecycle hooks.
- Evaluates observability via a metrics endpoint and logs on a PVC, with a simple autoscale path via HPA.
- Probes, resource requests, and minimal skeletons show readiness for real-world CKAD constraints.

Key Concepts
- ConfigMap/Secret integration, InitContainer tooling, PVC-backed logs, custom metrics exposure, readiness/liveness, HPA kinship, minimal YAML.

Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: feature-tester
  namespace: test-ns
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: feature-tester
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: feature-tester
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: init-tools
        image: alpine:3.18
        command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache httpie jq && mkdir -p /logs"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
      containers:
      - name: tester
        image: alpine:3.18
        command: ["sh", "-c", "while true; do for url in $(cat /etc/feature-endpoints/endpoints); do resp=$(http --ignore-stdin GET "$url" Authorization:"Bearer $(cat /secret/api_token)"); echo "$url -> $resp" >> /logs/$(date +%s).log; done; sleep 60; done"]
        env:
        - name: ENDPOINTS_CONFIG
          value: "/etc/feature-endpoints/endpoints"
        - name: TOKEN_SECRET
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: api-token
              key: token
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
          name: metrics
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "100m"
            memory: "128Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "256Mi"
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
      volumes:
      - name: logs
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: feature-tester-logs
      - name: feature-endpoints
        configMap:
          name: feature-endpoints
      - name: secret
        secret:
          secretName: api-token
      imagePullSecrets:
      - name: regcred
  
# Note: This is a minimal skeleton; real manifests should separate concerns (InitContainer, metrics, status storage) and handle errors gracefully.
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question evaluates your understanding of namespace-scoped automation, PVC usage, and secure scanning workflows within Kubernetes.

## Key Concepts
- Per-namespace CronJob with PVC mounts for manifests and logs
- Lightweight containerized scanner (e.g., trivy-lite)
- ConfigMap-based findings storage
- InitContainer for tool provisioning (jq, curl)
- Readiness and liveness probes on Job Pods
- Namespace NetworkPolicy for egress restrictions

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: manifest-scan
  namespace: example-ns
spec:
  schedule: "*/10 * * * *"
  successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  failedJobsHistoryLimit: 1
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          initContainers:
          - name: tools-installer
            image: busybox:1.36
            command:
            - sh
            - -c
            - |
              wget -q https://github.com/stedolan/jq/releases/download/jq-1.6/jq-linux64 -O /tmp/jq
              chmod +x /tmp/jq
              apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl
            volumeMounts:
            - name: tools
              mountPath: /tmp
          containers:
          - name: scanner
            image: trivy-lite:latest
            volumeMounts:
            - name: manifests
              mountPath: /manifests
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
            - name: tools
              mountPath: /tools
            command:
            - sh
            - -c
            - |
              export PATH=/tmp:$PATH
              for manifest in /manifests/*.yaml; do
                trivy scan --format json -o /logs/$(basename $manifest).json $manifest
              done
              kubectl get configmap security-scan -n example-ns -o yaml > /logs/configmap-backup.yaml
            readinessProbe:
              exec:
                command:
                - ls
                - /logs
              initialDelaySeconds: 5
              periodSeconds: 10
            livenessProbe:
              exec:
                command:
                - cat
                - /tmp/health
              initialDelaySeconds: 15
              periodSeconds: 20
          volumes:
          - name: manifests
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: manifest-pvc
          - name: logs
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: log-pvc
          - name: tools
            emptyDir: {}
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
```

## Trade-offs
- **PVC vs ConfigMap**: Using a PVC for logs allows for larger log volumes and retention, but requires storage provisioning. ConfigMaps are simpler but size-limited.
- **InitContainer vs Sidecar**: InitContainers run once per pod startup; sidecars run continuously. For a CronJob, InitContainers are more cost-effective.
- **NetworkPolicy**: Restricting egress improves security but may break updates if registries change. Consider using DNS whitelisting rather than specific IP ranges.
- **Probe timing**: Aggressive probes may cause premature failures; conservative settings increase job execution time.
- **CronJob frequency**: More frequent scans catch vulnerabilities faster but increase cluster load and API calls.

## Why This Is Asked
CKAD candidates must diagnose real issues with limited tools. This tests debugging flow, resource tuning, and readiness/liveness strategies.

## Key Concepts
- OOMKilled diagnosis through pod events and logs
- Resource requests/limits tuning and safety margins
- Probes (readiness and liveness) to recover from bad states

## Code Example
````yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-app
  namespace: prod
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: myrepo/web-app:latest
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: "512Mi"
            cpu: "500m"
          limits:
            memory: "1Gi"
            cpu: "1000m"
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 5
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 30
          periodSeconds: 10
````

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you validate changes in a staging environment before production?
- What trade-offs exist between higher requests/limits and cluster density?

## Why This Is Asked

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: ns-security-baseline
  namespace: <target-namespace>
spec:
  replicas: 1

      initContainers:
      - name: installer
        image: busybox
        command: ["sh","-c","apk add --no-cache curl jq || true"]

              key: token
```

## Why This Is Asked

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: image-processor
  namespace: batch
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      parallelism: 25
      completions: 500
      ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 3600
      backoffLimit: 3
      template:
        spec:
          initContainers:
            - name: seed-work
              image: busybox
              command: ["sh", "-c", "cp /config/files /work/"]
              volumeMounts:
                - name: work
                  mountPath: /work
          containers:
            - name: processor
              image: registry.example/image-processor:latest
              volumeMounts:
                - name: config
                  mountPath: /config
                - name: data
                  mountPath: /data
                - name: secrets
                  mountPath: /secrets/api
              readinessProbe: {"httpGet": {"path": "/healthz", "port": 8080}, "initialDelaySeconds": 5, "periodSeconds": 10}
              livenessProbe: {"httpGet": {"path": "/readyz", "port": 8080}, "initialDelaySeconds": 15, "periodSeconds": 20}
              securityContext:
                runAsNonRoot: true
                capabilities:
                  drop: ["ALL"]
          volumes:
            - name: config
              configMap:
                name: files-config
            - name: data
              persistentVolumeClaim:
                claimName: data-pvc
            - name: secrets
              secret:
                secretName: api-credentials
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
          imagePullSecrets:
            - name: regcred
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Question Matters for CKAD

This question validates mastery of **production-grade Kubernetes patterns** — not just textbook syntax. It combines seven CKAD concepts (CronJob, Job, InitContainer, ConfigMap, Secret, PVC, NetworkPolicy) in a realistic multi-tenant operational scenario.

## Key Concepts Tested

| Concept | Role in Pipeline |
|---------|-----------------|
| **CronJob** | Schedules periodic migrations with concurrency control |
| **Job** | Executes single migration attempt (created by CronJob) |
| **InitContainer** | Prepares SQL client before main container runs |
| **ConfigMap** | Versioned, injectable migration scripts without image rebuilds |
| **Secret** | Secure credential injection with namespace isolation |
| **PVC** | Persistent log storage for debugging and audit trail |
| **NetworkPolicy** | Enforces zero-trust network per namespace |

## Critical Design Decisions

1. **Why InitContainer for SQL client?**
   - Keeps main image minimal (security) and migration image separate from app image
   - Trade-off: adds startup latency and complexity

2. **Why PVC at /logs?**
   - Jobs are ephemeral; logs would be lost without persistence
   - Enables audit trail and post-mortem debugging

3. **Why NetworkPolicy egress restriction?**
   - Tenant database should only receive connections from migration Jobs
   - Prevents lateral movement in case of pod compromise

4. **Why probes on Job Pod?**
   - Liveness: ensures stuck jobs are restarted (but can cause issues with long migrations)
   - Readiness: typically irrelevant for Jobs, but included per question requirements

## Common Pitfalls Candidates Miss

- Forgetting `restartPolicy: OnFailure` (Jobs require explicit restart policy)
- Not handling ConfigMap subPath mounting (prevents live updates)
- Missing PVC lifecycle management (orphan storage, cost accumulation)
- NetworkPolicy blocking DNS (common exam/interview mistake)
- Not considering concurrent Job execution (data corruption risk)

## Real-World Extensions

- **Argo Workflows**: For complex multi-step migrations with retry logic
- **Flyway/ Liquibase**: Tool-based migrations with built-in versioning
- **External Secrets Operator**: Dynamic credential rotation without pod restarts
- **Cilium NetworkPolicy**: More expressive than standard K8s NetworkPolicy

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to safely patch CronJobs, leverage InitContainers for bootstrapping from ConfigMaps, enforce security context non-root, and apply sensible history limits. It also probes operational testing and rollback strategy for scheduled jobs.

## Key Concepts
- CronJob controls: concurrencyPolicy, history limits, startingDeadlineSeconds
- InitContainers and ConfigMaps for bootstrapping
- PodSecurityContext: runAsNonRoot
- Probes on Jobs' pods and resource requests/limits
- Testing and rollback of scheduled jobs

## Code Example
```yaml
# Minimal CronJob patch outline (conceptual)
apiVersion: batch/v1beta1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: db-backup
  namespace: nightly
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid
  startingDeadlineSeconds: 3600
  successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  failedJobsHistoryLimit: 1
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          serviceAccountName: backup-sa
          securityContext:
            runAsNonRoot: true
          initContainers:
            - name: init-backup
              image: busybox
              command: ["sh", "-c", "cp /config/backup.sh /backup/backup.sh"]
              volumeMounts:
                - name: backup-config
                  mountPath: /config
                - name: backups
                  mountPath: /backup
          containers:
            - name: backup
              image: backup-tool:latest
              resources:
                requests:
                  memory: "128Mi"
                  cpu: "100m"
                limits:
                  memory: "256Mi"
                  cpu: "500m"
              readinessProbe:
                httpGet:
                  path: /livez
                  port: 8080
              livenessProbe:
                httpGet:
                  path: /readyz
                  port: 8080
              volumeMounts:
                - name: backups
                  mountPath: /backups
          volumes:
            - name: backups
              persistentVolumeClaim:
                claimName: backups-pvc
            - name: backup-config
              configMap:
                name: backup-config
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you monitor backup duration and alert on failures?
- How would you handle a failed run without losing data?
